articleHeadline: Can International Travel Increase Your Risk of Tuberculosis?
articleSummary: Open Forum Infectious Diseases study (2010–2022) at a California federally qualified health centre serving a predominantly Asian American population found documented international travel associated with higher odds of TB test conversion. Among 5,668 patients with no prior TB history, at least one prior negative test, tested annually or every two years, those with documented international travel had 1.95 times the odds of converting from a negative to a positive TB test (95% CI 1.07–3.57) versus non-travelers. Most trips were to East and Southeast Asia, with >90% of recorded destinations in countries with medium or high TB prevalence. Two individuals were diagnosed with active TB after test conversion. The study cautions that travel is not proven causal and findings may not generalize beyond this single California centre. Routine TB testing for all travelers is not recommended; travel history should inform risk assessment and follow-up to distinguish latent infection from active disease.

articleHeadline: Warning signs of stroke and myocardial infarction in people infected with influenza.
articleSummary: Influenza infection elevates the risk of cardiovascular events, notably myocardial infarction and ischemic stroke, especially among the elderly and those with cardiovascular disease or chronic conditions. The inflammatory response from flu can destabilize atherosclerotic plaques, promote thrombosis, and increase myocardial oxygen demand, with pneumonia or respiratory failure reducing oxygen supply further increasing risk. Early after infection, studies show about a 6–10-fold rise in myocardial infarction risk and a 3–10-fold rise in stroke risk, based on specific studies. In Vietnam, a study of 598 elderly patients with coronary artery disease and/or heart failure followed for six months post-discharge found influenza vaccination reduced all-cause readmission (25.7% vs 41.2%), cardiovascular readmission (20.2% vs 35%), and all-cause mortality (1% vs 5.2%). Vaccination complements, not replaces, treatment; maintain blood pressure, lipids, and glucose control, and seek urgent care for chest pain, shortness of breath, fainting, or sudden weakness or speech difficulty. Emphasize vaccination and hygiene, especially for those 65+ and with chronic diseases.

articleSummary: Chittoor district, Aragonda, Andhra Pradesh, sees TB screening expansion through Apollo Foundation’s Total Health initiative with the state government. Apollo also provides nutrition kits to support treatment and follow-up.

articleHeadline: War Is Not Myanmar's Only Crisis — Floods, Hunger and Diseases Are Affecting Millions.
articleSummary: Nearly four million people remain displaced within Myanmar amid the civil conflict as floods and disease surge. In Sagaing's Shwebo corridor, floods compound hunger, with over 470,000 affected by July monsoon rains per WHO. Malaria and dengue cases have risen, and cholera outbreaks have emerged across the country, including Yangon in August and in flood regions such as Rakhine’s Sittwe and the Ayeyarwady delta. The dual crises drive up food prices and transport costs as competing factions extract tolls at checkpoints from Mandalay north to Shwebo. Inflation and supply disruptions leave farming households impoverished; fertilizer prices have surged, with cascading effects on next planting season. The junta intensifies control, using checkpoints, AI-enabled surveillance, and coercive conscription—more than 100,000 people reportedly recruited, with families paying to avoid service. Yangon faces security fears amid widespread hardship.

articleHeadline: A new strain of coronavirus could reach Russia — WHO.
articleSummary: The World Health Organization warns of rising global spread risk for the new coronavirus strain PJ.2.1. First detected in May 2026 in Ontario, Canada, PJ.2.1 has since spread to several continents, including Canada, the United States, and Europe. Health authorities say ongoing human movement increases the chance of introductions into new countries, including Russia. There are no clinical data showing a more severe illness with PJ.2.1 versus other recent SARS-CoV-2 variants; it has not been linked to higher rates of pneumonia, respiratory failure, or deaths. The main at‑risk group is people aged 60 and older. In Russia, a resident from Khabarovsk on holiday in Pattaya, Thailand, experienced a coma; preliminary diagnosis suggests infection with the new PJ.2.1 variant identified in the Kingdom of Thailand. The traveler, who went with his wife and two children, developed fever, seizures, and hallucinations days after arrival and remains comatose in a state hospital. His kidney donation to his daughter 16 years ago complicates his infection response.
